title: Structural Traps — Bargaining Problems
metadata_mapping: Existing concept and responsive asset conventions; no new schema, navigation, or publication action.

patterns.title: Bargaining Problems
patterns.domain: Strategic and game-theoretic problems; gains from agreement, distribution, alternatives, and bargaining procedures

sources.title: John F. Nash Jr., The Bargaining Problem (1950)
sources.supports: Two-person bargaining as mutually beneficial alternatives with distributional conflict; disagreement normalization; compact convex utility set; axiomatic product-of-gains characterization.
sources.read_method: Original paper opened on university host and downloaded; utility construction, disagreement baseline, assumptions, axioms, and product maximization derivation read in extracted text.
sources.boundary: The cooperative axiomatic benchmark does not specify the worked example’s negotiating procedure or predict acceptance of a mediator’s proposal. The example is a conditional facilitated agreement, rather than an equilibrium derived from a fully specified offer protocol. Symmetry and other axioms are modeling choices, not a universal justice standard.

sources.title: Ariel Rubinstein, Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model (1982)
sources.supports: Distinction between axiomatic and strategic approaches; alternating proposals, preferences over share and delay, complete information, and perfect-equilibrium sensitivity to patience and first mover.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted original scanned paper opened and downloaded. First three pages rendered and OCR read, including introduction, preference assumptions, fixed-discount characterization, complete-information caveat, and subgame perfection.
sources.boundary: The article discusses only the constant-discount version for procedural comparison. Its alternating-offer results are not applied to the hypothetical bicycle-price agreement, and no numerical Rubinstein outcome is claimed.

sources.title: Alvin E. Roth, J. Keith Murnighan, and Françoise Schoumaker, The Deadline Effect in Bargaining: Some Experimental Evidence (1988)
sources.supports: Four laboratory bargaining experiments showed agreements concentrated near deadlines and substantial disagreement; much timing analysis was retrospective.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted scanned original report opened and downloaded; first three pages rendered and OCR read, covering study motivation, laboratory timing, agreement distribution, design limitations, and binary-lottery environment.
sources.boundary: Laboratory observations are not a universal field prediction or a randomized estimate of the effect of imposing tighter deadlines. Article uses no empirical percentage as a target for the invented negotiation.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when agreement creates a shared gain but competing claims prevent its division, then separate feasible deals, bargaining procedures, alternatives, and fairness judgments.
use_when: Which prices can both prefer to walking away?
goals: Recognize the concrete predicament before terminology.
Preserve defining assumptions and distinctions without calculations.
Evaluate intervention authority, costs, residual risks, and changed assumptions.
mechanisms: Establish real alternatives and select acceptable enforceable terms within the overlap.
Private limits may be hard to learn. No overlap requires a changed package or no sale; fairness remains open.

example_structure.scenario: Known condition and ownership of one secondhand bicycle; fixed included package, credible known acceptance limits and outside options, rejection available, earlier discussion nonbinding, single sale. A price in the overlap is acceptable but not uniquely fair. Price ordering only; no invented monetary utilities.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Establish real alternatives and select acceptable enforceable terms within the overlap.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Private limits may be hard to learn. No overlap requires a changed package or no sale; fairness remains open.
example_structure.evidence: Hypothetical scenario and stipulated continuation; no expected result presented as measured outcome. Qualitative ranking and ordering replace illustrative arithmetic.

No overlap requires a changed package or no sale; fairness remains open.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. Regions are ordered by increasing price without numerical distances. Overlap makes a mutually acceptable sale possible, but selects no uniquely fair price. The example assumes known acceptance limits and a feasible exchange.

patterns.evidence_boundary: Foundational definitions and formal results retain their assumptions. Empirical studies retain setting and design limitations. Examples and suggested practical responses are original editorial synthesis. Expected familiarity is an editorial judgment, not a comprehension-study finding.
